data: The larger and inner of Mars's two moons — irregular potato-shaped body just 22 km across at its widest. Phobos orbits Mars every 7 hours 39 minutes, faster than Mars itself rotates, so from the Martian surface it rises in the west and sets in the east twice per Martian day. Its orbit is decaying at ~2 cm per year; in 30–50 million years tidal forces will either tear it apart into a temporary ring or crash it into the planet. Japan's MMX mission (launch ~2026) will return surface samples.

Heavily-cratered carbonaceous chondrite-like body, possibly a captured asteroid or accretion remnant; surface dominated by the 9 km Stickney crater and parallel grooves likely tied to ejecta from that impact.
Mars Express — ESA, 2010 (sub-100 m altitude flyby)
Phobos orbits Mars at just 9,377 km — below the synchronous altitude, so it is tidally accelerated INWARD and will impact Mars in ~40 million years.
Phobos's perihelion-aphelion swing is tiny but it circles Mars three times per Martian day — the most-orbits-per-parent-day moon in the system.
Half the longest diameter of the orbit ellipse — and the single number that sets the orbital period.
